demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Daniel Mercer was 54, a married forester who had spent most of his adult life in the woods, reading terrain, marking stands, and moving easily through rough country that other people tended to avoid. Until the accident, that steadiness had been part of how he understood himself. The event happened on a work site in late summer, when he was walking a narrow cutline with a crew and another man was moving nearby in uneven ground. Daniel had turned, misjudged the space between them, and in the moment of movement and impact the other man was seriously injured. Daniel did not describe it as a dramatic split-second in which everything changed so much as a single terrible mistake that replayed in his mind with relentless clarity. What stayed with him was the shock of the other man on the ground, the immediacy of the injury, and the awful sense that he had been the one to cause it.

In the weeks after, Daniel found that any reminder of injured bodies could pull him straight back to that day. Physical pain in his own body, even something ordinary like a sharp twinge or an ache after a long day, could catch him off guard and make the whole memory feel close again. If he saw someone limping, bracing a shoulder, or moving with the guarded stiffness of pain, he would notice it at once and feel his attention lock onto them. He also found himself unsettled by physical proximity in a way that felt new and humiliating to him. When another person came too near on a trail, in a store aisle, or in the cramped space of a work truck, he became tense and watchful, aware of bodies in space and of how quickly a mistake could happen. He could no longer trust a simple pass-by without checking distances, angles, and hands.

The memory itself came back to him in a bodily way that was hard for him to explain. When it surfaced, he would feel as if his own body had dropped back into the position he had been in at the moment of the injury, shoulders tight, head turned, muscles fixed as though he could not quite move out of it. He would feel his jaw clench and his chest go hard, as if his body were holding the accident in place. Along with that came intense rage, directed first at himself for what he had done and then at the cruelty of the whole thing, the single mistake that had injured another man and could not be taken back. At other moments, what rose up was grief so heavy it felt overwhelming, not only for the injured man but for the version of himself who had once trusted his own skill and judgment. He said that remembering the event did not feel like recalling a story; it felt like being struck by all of it at once.

Over time, Daniel came to believe that there was something in him that made the event happen. He did not talk about it as bad luck. He talked about it as a flaw in himself, something intrinsic that made him dangerous or untrustworthy in a way others might not see. Because of that, he had trouble relying on himself. Decisions that once came naturally now felt suspect, as if he might miss something crucial and only realize it after harm had already been done. The work that had defined him for decades became hard to inhabit in the same way. He was no longer certain he was capable of the things that had given his life shape: moving confidently in the woods, handling responsibility in the field, and doing the practical tasks that once made him feel useful and precise.

That sense of being unable to relax followed him into the rest of his life. Even at home, in what should have been a safe place, he remained keyed up, unable to settle fully. He found himself watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him, an alertness that surprised him because it came up in ordinary situations with strangers as well as in busier public places. If someone approached him unexpectedly, especially in a parking lot or on a path, he would track their movement, their hands, their pace, and whether they seemed to be closing the distance too quickly. His wife noticed that he had become harder to draw into ordinary ease. He remained present, but not fully at rest, as if a part of him were always scanning.

At work, the changes were especially difficult. As a forester, Daniel still had to be around other people in the field and move through spaces where bodies, tools, and uneven ground created constant practical risks. He found himself drawn into careful monitoring of others' positions and too aware of every approach from behind or from the side. He also became more reluctant to stay close when a worker had an injury or complained of pain, because those moments could send him back to the accident with such force. The job that had once anchored him now felt like a place where reminders could appear without warning. By the time he sought help, he was troubled by how often he was on edge, how strongly the memories could return in his body, and how deeply he feared that he was no longer the man he had been. What brought him in now was the growing realization that he could not keep carrying the accident alone, and what he most hoped for was some way to trust himself again without feeling that every close pass, every stranger, and every twinge of pain was about to bring the whole thing back.
